learn.intro: Propaganda, censorship, the secret police and control of culture and religion kept the Communist Party in power for over seventy years. How did these methods change from Lenin to Gorbachev, and what happened when controls were relaxed?

sections.title: 1. Media, propaganda and religion

blocks.p: State control of mass media: the Bolsheviks closed opposition newspapers within days of taking power. Glavlit (1922) censored all publications, and Pravda and Izvestia carried the party line. Posters, agitprop trains, film and later radio spread propaganda.

The personality cult of Stalin grew from his fiftieth birthday in December 1929: he was presented as Lenin's true heir, the 'father of the peoples' and the architect of victory. History was rewritten — the Short Course history of the party (1938) became compulsory reading.

The treatment of religion: church and state were separated in January 1918 and church property seized. The League of the Godless (1925) ran anti-religious propaganda, and the 1929 Law on Religious Associations banned religious teaching and charity. By 1939 only a few hundred Orthodox churches remained open. In 1943 Stalin allowed the Orthodox Church to elect a patriarch to win support during the war.

Khrushchev launched a new anti-religious campaign (1958–64) that closed about half of the remaining churches. Brezhnev was less aggressive towards religion, but tightened controls on writers and dissidents — for example the trial of Sinyavsky and Daniel (1966) — and after the Prague Spring (1968).

evidence: December 1929: Stalin's fiftieth birthday launches the cult.

sections.title: 2. The secret police and attacks on opponents

blocks.p: The political police changed name but not purpose: Cheka (1917), GPU and OGPU (1922–23), NKVD (from 1934), and the KGB (from 1954). The Gulag system of labour camps was organised from 1930 and held around 2.5 million people in camps and colonies by 1953.

The roles of Yagoda, Yezhov and Beria: Genrikh Yagoda led the NKVD from 1934 and organised the first show trial, then was himself tried and shot (1938). Nikolai Yezhov ran the Great Terror of 1937–38 and was shot in 1940. Lavrenty Beria (from 1938) reduced the mass arrests but ran the camps and wartime deportations of whole nationalities; he was shot after Stalin's death in 1953.

Liberalisation under Khrushchev 1953–64: about 1.2 million prisoners were amnestied in 1953, millions more were released and many victims rehabilitated after 1956. The KGB was placed firmly under party control. But limits remained: the Hungarian rising was crushed (1956) and strikers at Novocherkassk were shot (1962).

Suppression of dissidents 1965–82 and the significance of Andropov: as KGB chairman (1967–82) Yuri Andropov used exile, psychiatric hospitals and forced emigration rather than mass terror. Solzhenitsyn was expelled (1974) and the physicist Andrei Sakharov exiled to Gorky (1980). Samizdat (self-published writing) such as the Chronicle of Current Events spread news of abuses.
1982–91: the KGB continued to monitor popular discontent through informers and reports, but under glasnost Sakharov was released (December 1986) and protest became open.

evidence: 1953: Beria shot; amnesty of about 1.2 million.

sections.title: 3. The state and cultural change

blocks.p: Proletkult and the avant-garde (1917–early 1930s): the Proletkult movement tried to create a new working-class culture. Avant-garde artists such as Malevich, the poet Mayakovsky and the film-maker Eisenstein (Battleship Potemkin, 1925) experimented with new forms.

Socialist Realism (from 1934): the First Congress of Soviet Writers made Socialist Realism compulsory — art had to be optimistic, easy to understand and show the building of socialism. All writers had to belong to the Union of Soviet Writers. After the war the Zhdanov decrees (1946) attacked writers such as Akhmatova and Zoshchenko.

Nonconformity from the 1950s: in Khrushchev's 'Thaw' some criticism was allowed — Solzhenitsyn's One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962) described the Gulag. But Pasternak was forced to refuse the Nobel Prize (1958) for Doctor Zhivago, and Khrushchev attacked abstract art at the Manège exhibition (1962). Under Brezhnev an unofficial open-air art show was bulldozed (1974).

The impact of the breakdown of traditional controls 1985–91: glasnost allowed banned works such as Doctor Zhivago (published 1988) and films critical of Stalinism such as Repentance (1987). Magazines exposed the crimes of the past, rock music and Western culture spread, and the party lost control of the stories Soviet people told about their own history.

evidence: 1962: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich.
1988: Doctor Zhivago published in the USSR.

misconceptions.wrong: Terror was the only way the regime controlled people.
misconceptions.right: Propaganda, rewards, education and genuine belief mattered as well.
He released millions, but crushed Hungary (1956) and Novocherkassk (1962) and attacked the Church.
Repression was targeted: exile, psychiatric hospitals and expulsion of dissidents.
Churches were closed, but belief survived and Stalin used the Church in the war.

matching.title: Match the person to their role

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of liberalisation under Khrushchev, and its limits.
evidence.model: About 1.2 million prisoners were amnestied in 1953 and many victims rehabilitated after the Secret Speech (1956); the KGB was put under party control. But Hungary was crushed in 1956 and strikers were shot at Novocherkassk in 1962.

flashcards.q: How was the Stalin cult created?
flashcards.a: From his fiftieth birthday (1929): posters, rewritten history (Short Course 1938), Stalin as Lenin's heir and 'father of the peoples'.

flashcards.q: How was religion treated from Stalin to Brezhnev?
flashcards.a: Stalin: churches closed, 1929 law, then wartime concession (1943). Khrushchev: renewed campaign 1958–64. Brezhnev: less aggressive, controlled through the Council for Religious Affairs.
Yagoda: first show trial, shot 1938. Yezhov: Great Terror 1937–38, shot 1940. Beria: ended mass arrests but ran the camps and deportations, shot 1953.
KGB chairman 1967–82: targeted repression of dissidents (exile, psychiatric hospitals, expulsion) instead of mass terror; then leader 1982–84.
From 1934: art must be optimistic, simple and celebrate socialism; enforced through the Union of Soviet Writers.

flashcards.q: What was the impact of the breakdown of controls 1985–91?
flashcards.a: Banned works published, Stalin's crimes exposed, Western culture spread — the party lost control of history and public opinion.

checklist.text: I can explain how the state used the media, propaganda and the Stalin cult.
I can judge how far the treatment of religion changed under Stalin, Khrushchev and Brezhnev.
I can assess the roles of Yagoda, Yezhov, Beria and Andropov, and the extent of liberalisation under Khrushchev.
I can explain how state control of culture changed from Proletkult to glasnost.
